sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ninlil** (*ninlil*) — Wind, Air · Lady of the wind — belongs to the Mesopotamian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Wind, Air". The name means "Lady of the wind"[^1].

**Ninlil** is the Sumerian goddess of the wind and the air, the consort of Enlil and queen of the Mesopotamian pantheon. Her name, written 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤, simply means 'Lady of the Wind' — *nin* ('lady, queen') plus *lil* ('wind, air'). Where Enlil commands the storm and the decree of kingship, Ninlil is the gentler sovereign of the moving air itself: the breath that fills the lungs, the breeze that carries pollen, and the unseen presence that links heaven and earth.

This temple honours Ninlil as both **queen** and **mother**. She is the mother of Nanna/Sîn the moon, of Nergal lord of the underworld, of Ninazu, and of Enbilulu the canal inspector. The myth *Enlil and Ninlil* (ETCSL 1.2.1) weaves her story together with the theological geography of Mesopotamia: even the queen of the air must know the underworld, because descent and generation are inseparable in the Sumerian cosmos.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ninlil** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/ninlil/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *ninlil* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.
Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Cuneiform as **𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤**. Etymologically it means "Lady of the wind"[^1].

The ASCII form *ninlil* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ninlil** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **n** → **N** — Same, capitalized
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/nɪnˈlɪl/** — Sumerian Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Nin-** — Voiceless alveolar stop [n] plus close front vowel [ɪ] — the Sumerian word for 'lady, queen,' marking her rank in the pantheon.
- **-lil** — Lateral approximant [l] repeated around a short [ɪ] — the Sumerian word for 'wind' or 'air,' the element she embodies and governs.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'nin-LIL' — stress the second syllable and let the name end with a light, breathy lilt, like wind passing through reeds.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sumerian** — 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤 (dnin-lil₂), 'lady of the wind/air' — queen of the Sumerian gods and consort of Enlil
- **Akkadian** — Mullil / Mullissu, the Akkadian rendering of Ninlil, later identified with the consort of Aššur
- **Cuneiform** — 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤, written with the divine determinative 𒀭 (dingir) prefixed to the name

Ninlil is Tier 2: the canonical Unicode restoration is identical to the ASCII form, with no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter preserved. The name is the same in both forms; what the temple protects is not a phonological mark but the proper-name capitalization and the scholarly framing of a Sumerian theonym. Standard Assyriology writes Ninlil; PuniCodex presents the plain form as a baseline restoration of a Mesopotamian divine name.

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in Cuneiform as **𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤** — Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform, attested Sumerian / Old Babylonian – Neo-Assyrian, c. 2600–600 BCE, in Mesopotamia. The script is written left-to-right / top-to-bottom.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Ninlil* (Sumerian logogram + Akkadian scholarly), giving the normalized reading /ˈnin.lil/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sumerogram NIN.LÍL (𒊩𒌆𒆤), 'lady of the wind'
- Prefixed with divine determinative 𒀭
- Consort of Enlil and mother of Nanna/Sîn

sections.body:
**Ninlil** is the Sumerian goddess of the wind and the air, the consort of Enlil and queen of the Mesopotamian pantheon. Her name, written 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤, simply means 'Lady of the Wind' — *nin* ('lady, queen') plus *lil* ('wind, air'). Where Enlil commands the storm and the decree of kingship, Ninlil is the gentler sovereign of the moving air itself: the breath that fills the lungs, the breeze that carries pollen, and the unseen presence that links heaven and earth.

This temple honours Ninlil as both **queen** and **mother**. She is the mother of Nanna/Sîn the moon, of Nergal lord of the underworld, of Ninazu, and of Enbilulu the canal inspector. The myth *Enlil and Ninlil* (ETCSL 1.2.1) weaves her story together with the theological geography of Mesopotamia: even the queen of the air must know the underworld, because descent and generation are inseparable in the Sumerian cosmos.[^1]

### The Wind

The moving air itself — breath, breeze, and the life-giving currents that cross the Mesopotamian plain.

### Queenship

Consort of Enlil and queen of the gods; the divine matriarch from whom lunar and netherworld powers descend.

### The Crescent Moon

Mother of Nanna/Sîn; the lunar crescent is her descendant's sign, linking wind-queen to night-light.

### Descent and Return

The mythic journey into the underworld that generates new gods and new seasons of life.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Ninlil concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **Wind and breath** — The invisible air that sustains life and carries the voice of command
- **Crescent moon** — The sign of her son Nanna/Sîn, the moon god
- **Gate and canal** — The liminal places where Ninlil meets Enlil in the myth of their union
- **Grain and reed** — The crops that bend in the wind and depend on air-borne pollination
- **Horned crown** — The crown of divine queenship worn by the chief consort of the king of gods

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ninlil's myths are stories of **boundary-crossing**: the wind that moves between worlds, the queen who descends into darkness, and the mother whose children personify moon, death, water, and order. She is not a passive consort; she is the necessary counterpart without whom Enlil's kingship would be incomplete.[^1]

### Enlil and Ninlil (The Sacred Marriage)

The Sumerian poem *Enlil and Ninlil* (ETCSL 1.2.1) tells how the young god Enlil saw Ninlil by the canal at Nippur and desired her. After he impregnated her, the assembled gods banished him from the city for his offence. Ninlil followed him into exile. In the underworld Enlil met her three times in disguise — as the gatekeeper, the river-man, and the ferryman — and each union produced a child: Nergal, Ninazu, and Enbilulu. The story explains the origin of three underworld or chthonic deities and makes theological sense of descent: even the king and queen of the air must generate the powers of the depths.[^2]

### Mother of the Moon (Maternity)

Ninlil is the mother of **Nanna/Sîn**, the moon god, and in some traditions also of **Inanna/Ištar** and **Utu/Shamash**. The moon's regular cycle becomes an extension of the air-queen's generative power: what moves unseen by day shines by night. Royal hymns from Ur and Nippur invoke Ninlil alongside Enlil as the divine parents who legitimate the king and protect the city.

### Ninlil in the Netherworld (Descent)

In the myth *The Descent of Enlil* and related hymnic traditions, Ninlil accompanies or follows Enlil into the netherworld. Her presence there is not punishment but cosmic necessity: the queen of the upper air must also know the lower world, so that the breath of life and the breath of the dead remain in relation. This descent mirrors the better-known descent of Inanna, but it is told through the lens of divine sovereignty rather than individual transformation.

### The Temples of Ninlil (Cult)

Ninlil's principal cult centre was at **Nippur**, where she shared the great sanctuary complex with Enlil. Sumerian temple hymns praise her house and link her authority to the Ekur, the 'Mountain House' of Enlil. In later Assyrian religion she was equated with **Mullissu**, the consort of Aššur, and her cult travelled with Assyrian kingship to cities such as Nineveh and Assur. Her worship thus spans Sumer, Babylonia, and Assyria across more than two millennia.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Unicode form **Ninlil** is a baseline restoration: standard Assyriology writes the name without diacritics, and the canonical PuniCodex form preserves that plain spelling while asserting proper-name status. In Akkadian and Assyrian sources Ninlil was identified with **Mullissu** (also spelled Mulliltu), the consort of the national god Aššur. In Hittite and Hurrian milieus her functions were partly absorbed by the great goddess **Hepat** and by local consort deities. Greek and Roman writers had no direct equivalent for Ninlil, though her rank as queen of the gods and her association with air invite loose comparison with Hera or Juno; the comparison, however, is typological rather than historical.[^1]

Within the Mesopotamian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[adad|Adad]], [[anu|Anû]], [[apsu|Apsû]], [[ashur|Aššur]], [[dumuzid|Dumuzid]], and [[ea|Ēa]].

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Ninlil survives in Assyriological scholarship and in the modern recovery of Sumerian religion through ETCSL and the great lexical projects of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. She is less famous in popular culture than her daughter Ištar or her consort Enlil, yet her role as wind-queen and mother of lunar and netherworld powers makes her essential to any coherent picture of the Mesopotamian pantheon. The name **Ninlil** is sometimes adopted by fantasy settings and neopagan circles as an emblem of air, sovereignty, and the unseen. PuniCodex presents the plain ASCII form not as a deficiency but as a philologically honest baseline: there is no recovered diacritic to restore, only the name itself to remember.[^1]

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Cuneiform tablets from Nippur, Ur, and Assur attest Ninlil's cult from the Early Dynastic period into the first millennium BCE. The Ekur sanctuary at Nippur, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania and Iraqi teams, preserves the architectural setting of her worship alongside Enlil. Assyrian royal inscriptions from Nineveh and Assur name Mullissu/Ninlil as the divine consort who legitimises the king, while cylinder seals and votive objects depict her wearing the horned crown of divine queenship.[^1]

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.

sections.label: Cuneiform Sources
sections.body: Ninlil’s name and cult are attested across three millennia of cuneiform writing. The Sumerian poem *Enlil and Ninlil* (ETCSL 1.2.1) supplies the fullest narrative, recounting her unions that conceive Nanna/Sîn, Nergal, Ninazu and Enbilulu within the theological geography of Nippur and the netherworld. Royal inscriptions and temple hymns from Ur and Assur invoke her as *dnin-lil₂* (𒀭𒊩𒌆𒆤), usually paired with Enlil, while administrative tablets record regular offerings at her shrines. God lists such as *An = Anum* fix her rank in the canonical Mesopotamian pantheon.[^1][^2][^3]

sections.label: Enūma Eliš
sections.body: The late Babylonian *Enūma Eliš* celebrates Marduk’s defeat of Tiamat, yet it rests on an older theological architecture in which Enlil, Ninlil’s consort, embodies supreme authority. By the first millennium BCE Ninlil had been identified with Mullissu, the Assyrian consort of Aššur, and her lineage was woven into the imperial pantheon the epic proclaims. Thus the poem does not stage Ninlil directly; it testifies to the sovereignty she anchors—air, queenship and the transmission of kingship from Sumer through Babylon to Assyria.[^1][^2]

sources.citation: Foster, Benjamin R. Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature. CDL Press, 2005.
Dalley, Stephanie. Myths from Mesopotamia: Creation, the Flood, Gilgamesh, and Others. Oxford University Press, 2000.

sections.label: Atra-Ḫasīs
sections.body: In the Akkadian *Atra-Ḫasīs* epic, Enlil’s anger unleashes the flood that nearly extinguishes humankind. Ninlil’s domain—the air, wind and breath of life—is precisely the element the deluge violates. When the gods settle for a regulated human population and institutions that channel mortality, they restore the cosmic conditions Ninlil governs. Her queenship of the air therefore underwrites the postdiluvian order the narrative establishes.[^1][^2]

sources.citation: Foster, Benjamin R. Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature. CDL Press, 2005.
Dalley, Stephanie. Myths from Mesopotamia: Creation, the Flood, Gilgamesh, and Others. Oxford University Press, 2000.
Jacobsen, Thorkild. The Treasures of Darkness: A History of Mesopotamian Religion. Yale University Press, 1976.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Air is the most taken-for-granted element. We do not see it until it moves, do not value it until it fails. Ninlil is the goddess of that taken-for-grantedness made sacred: the breath in the body, the wind in the grain, the medium that carries both speech and storm. Her marriage to Enlil is the marriage of power to atmosphere: he decrees, she enables; he commands, she circulates.

To restore the name *Ninlil* is therefore to restore attention. There is no macron or circumflex to argue over here; the philological work is simply to keep the name from flattening into noise. In a world of brandable deities, a Tier-2 name is easily dismissed. But Ninlil reminds us that not every god needs a diacritic to matter. Some names carry their distinction in the thing they name: the wind itself, invisible and everywhere.[^1]

sources.citation: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, Oxford Oriental Institute, 1998.
